problem: End-to-end RL navigation policies are fragile and lack a consistent spatial representation, while SLAM/visual odometry drift in repetitive scenes and depend on stored maps. Raw pixels, raw coordinates or detector outputs give RL agents poor generalization and planning around occluded paths.
motivation: Mammalian entorhinal grid cells give a compact, periodic, multi-scale position code that supports path integration and vector-based navigation. The authors hypothesize that feeding such a code, inferred from egocentric motion and visual landmarks, into an RL policy yields efficient and robust navigation without explicit maps.
key_idea: Train a PPO policy on grid-cell-like periodic position embeddings (plus head-direction sin/cos), and replace ground-truth grid activations with an LSTM encoder that predicts them from landmark/DINO visual features and velocity.
insight: Grid codes as policy input let agents learn a viable path around a wall where normalized (x,y) input fails, and beat raw pixels and YOLO in MiniWorld complex scenes. The paper notes normalized position gets comparable reward to pixels/YOLO but a much lower success rate, suggesting it avoids obstacles but fails to find a path. In Gazebo, YOLO with LiDAR and a recurrent policy trains faster and more stably, with grid cells matching its success rate only at 1M steps. Evidence is qualitative: the reported numbers are in figures, and the learned encoder is validated only by heatmaps of predicted versus true activations.
method: Grid cell encoder: 72 ideal hexagonal grid activations (cos-sum with scales, 12 phase shifts, 2 rotations) used as supervised targets; a 2-layer MLP + LSTM + MLP head predicts them and a sin/cos heading (74-d output).
Head direction encoding: orientation θ is encoded as [sinθ, cosθ] as an analogue of head-direction cells.
Visual landmark input: AprilTag IDs and corner coordinates (38-d + velocity) in MiniWorld; DINOv2 384-d features + velocity in Gazebo with real objects (chair, plant, human).

PPO policy: Stable-Baselines3 PPO (recurrent LSTM PPO in Gazebo) on the 74-d grid+heading vector, velocity, and 36-d LiDAR in Gazebo; continuous acceleration actions (linear, angular) integrated into velocity.
Reward: sparse goal reward r_g = 1-0.2*steps/max_steps, collision -0.1, step -0.01.

Two-stage encoder distillation: train a policy on ground-truth grid codes, roll out policy and random trajectories (20k×400 steps MiniWorld, 1,280×1,000 Gazebo), train the LSTM with MSE as a drop-in replacement.
Baselines: raw normalized position+orientation, raw 96×96 image (CNN), YOLO goal detection, all with velocity (and LiDAR in Gazebo).

setting.backbone: PPO / recurrent PPO policy (trained from scratch) + LSTM grid cell encoder; DINOv2 (frozen) feature extractor in Gazebo
setting.model_size: 0.9M total in MiniWorld; 87.06M total in Gazebo (mostly the DINOv2 extractor)
setting.training_data: RL interaction in simulation; encoder trained on 20,000 trajectories × 400 steps (MiniWorld) and 1,280 × 1,000 steps (Gazebo) collected from policy and random agents
setting.observation: front-facing RGB (via AprilTag or DINOv2 features), linear/angular velocity, 36-d LiDAR in Gazebo
setting.action_space: continuous linear and angular acceleration, integrated into velocity (Twist in Gazebo, arc-based pose update in MiniWorld)
setting.privileged: Ground-truth grid activations used to train the initial policy and as encoder targets; the deployed variant uses the learned encoder. Fixed goal location and fixed environment layouts.

numbers_note: Results are only in figures (bar charts of reward/success rate/normalized steps); only text claims are given (99% simple, >94% complex), with no table values. The task is a custom goal-reaching task, not a standard benchmark.
results: The abstract claims 99% success in simple rooms and >94% in complex floorplans with occluded paths, with more efficient distance-normalized steps than raw-position, raw-image and YOLO baselines. In Gazebo, YOLO trained fastest and most stably, with grid cells comparable at 1M steps. The learned encoder reproduces the ground-truth grid patterns qualitatively.
limitations: Evaluated only in two simple custom simulated environments with a fixed goal and fixed layout, no real robot, and no standard benchmarks; metrics are given only in figures.

Depends on ground-truth grid activations for distillation and on known landmarks/fixed environments; the encoder is trained per scene, so zero-shot generalization is untested, and the Gazebo model is large (87M with DINOv2).
Grid-encoded Gazebo paths show cusps from incomplete convergence at 1M steps; the YOLO baseline was equal or better in Gazebo.
builds_on: Banino et al. vector-based navigation with grid cells
